paragraphs: I suppose that men have reached the point where the obstacles to their survival in the state of nature prove stronger than the resources each individual has for staying alive in that state. That original condition can then no longer continue, and the human race would perish unless it changed its way of living.

But men cannot create new forces; they can only combine and direct the ones that exist. So the only way they have to preserve themselves is to form, by joining together, a sum of forces large enough to overcome the resistance. They must set these forces in motion through a single driving power and make them act in concert.

This sum of forces can arise only when several persons come together. But the force and liberty of each man are the chief instruments of his self-preservation. How can he commit them to the group without harming his own interests and neglecting the care he owes to himself? In terms of my present subject, this difficulty can be stated as follows —

“The problem is to find a form of association that will defend and protect the person and goods of each associate with the whole common force, and in which each, while uniting with all, still obeys only himself and remains as free as before.” This is the fundamental problem to which the _Social Contract_ provides the solution.

The clauses of this contract are so determined by the nature of the act that the slightest change would make them empty and ineffective. So, although they have perhaps never been formally stated, they are the same everywhere and are everywhere tacitly accepted and recognized. This continues until the social compact is violated; then each person regains his original rights and resumes his natural liberty, while losing the conventional liberty for the sake of which he gave it up.

Properly understood, these clauses can be reduced to one: the total transfer of each associate, with all his rights, to the whole community. For, in the first place, since each gives himself completely, the conditions are the same for everyone; and since they are the same for everyone, no one has any interest in making them burdensome to others.

Moreover, because the transfer is made without reserve, the union is as perfect as it can be, and no associate has anything further to claim. For if individuals kept certain rights, there would be no common superior to judge between them and the public. Each, being his own judge on one point, would soon ask to be his own judge on all. The state of nature would continue, and the association would inevitably become either ineffective or tyrannical.

Finally, each man, in giving himself to all, gives himself to nobody. And since there is no associate over whom he does not gain the same right that he yields to others over himself, he gains the equivalent of everything he loses, along with more force to preserve what he has.
If, then, we set aside everything in the social compact that is not essential to it, we shall find that it comes down to these terms —
_“Each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will, and, as one body, we receive each member as an indivisible part of the whole.”_

At once, in place of the individual person of each party to the contract, this act of association creates a moral and collective body. It is made up of as many members as the assembly has votes, and from this act it receives its unity, its common identity, its life and its will. This public person, formed by the union of all the others, was formerly called a _city_,[1] and is now called a _Republic_ or _body politic_. Its members call it the _State_ when it is passive, the _Sovereign_ when it is active, and a _Power_ when they compare it with others like itself. Those who are associated in it are collectively called the _people_, and individually are called _citizens_, as sharing in the sovereign power, and _subjects_, as being under the laws of the State. But these terms are often confused and used for one another; it is enough to know how to tell them apart when they are used precisely.

The same mistake once cost the Carthaginians dearly. I have never read of the title of citizens being given to the subjects of any prince, not even the ancient Macedonians or the English of today, although they are nearer to liberty than anyone else. The French alone everywhere casually take up the name of citizens, because, as their dictionaries show, they have no idea of its meaning; otherwise, in usurping it, they would be guilty of the crime of _lèse-majesté_. Among them, the name expresses a virtue, not a right. When Bodin spoke of our citizens and townsmen, he made a bad blunder in taking the one class for the other. M. d’Alembert avoided the error, and in his article on Geneva he clearly distinguished the four orders of men (or even five, counting mere foreigners) who live in our town, of which only two make up the Republic. No other French writer, to my knowledge, has understood the real meaning of the word citizen.
